newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union halts talks with Chrysler.
newsitem.headline: Canada union halts talks with Chrysler.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers late Monday halted talks with Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian unit because of a lack of progress on the key issue of shifting work to outside companies and warned that a strike looked more likely.
"We're not moving any further until we resolve this issue," CAW President Buzz Hargrove told a short news conference.
Hargrove said it would now be difficult to conclude an agreement on all issues by the Tuesday strike deadline.
"The clock has become our enemy and it is very difficult for us to conclude an agreement on all issues ahead of 11:59 (EDT) on Tuesday," Hargrove said.

Chrysler officials said they remained optimistic that they could avert a strike. "We're still relatively optimistic things can be resolved prior to the strike deadline, a little over 24 hours away," said Othmar Stein, a spokesman for Chrysler Canada Ltd.
Stein said there was room for the company to move on the issue of outsourcing, or contracting work out, but that it was tied to other issues which the CAW had stalled on.
"There is always room to move on any of these issues but again it depends on how they tie into other issues of equal importance to us," he said.
Stein would not specify what those issues were.

Hargrove left after a short press conference for a caucus with the heads of the various committees of the union and said he would talk to Chrysler's lead negotiator Ken Francese about any possible further movement on outside suppliers and whether talks could resume.
The union has said its 12,600 Chrysler workers will strike the carmaker if an agreement was not reached by the deadline.
A collective agreement with Chrysler will become the framework for negotiations between the union and the Canadian units of General Motors Corp. and Ford Motor Co..

Hargrove said Chrysler's latest proposal on shifting work to outside companies, presented to the union on Sunday afternoon, recognised the principle of work ownership, but did not limit the automaker's ability to contract out the work.
"We own the work. The next step has to be that we have some say in what happens to it," said Hargrove.

"It (Chrysler) does now recognise the principle, in writing, of work ownership. But you could drive a truck through the language after that. So we are still an awful long ways apart," Hargrove said on Sunday during a break in bargaining.

CAW officials said work is owned by the union when workers are "producing quality products in a productive manner at reasonably low cost and (the company is) making a reasonable profit." Hargrove said once the company recognises work ownership, it follows that it cannot contract out the work without replacing it with other jobs.
Chrysler's Francese was unavailable on Monday but said on Sunday that he planned to meet again on the outsourcing issue and expected to begin closing the gap between the two sides.
"We're going to have more discussion on that and hopefully we'll be a lot closer at the end to resolving that issue," Francese said.
Hargrove said he had not expected Chrysler to concede the work ownership issue before a strike, but the early move to do so was only the first step toward controlling outsourcing.
"If you're looking down that tunnel, you'll see a little small light, but boy, it is faint," said Hargrove.
Hargrove said the union will not budge from its commitment to restrict outsourcing and that the talks cannot advance until the issue is settled.
